title: One Street, Six Hours, Three Paints: A Limited-Palette Study of Light
description: Six paintings of the same street corner at six different hours, using only ultramarine, burnt sienna, yellow ochre and white. What a limited palette teaches about local colour, light, shadow temperature and value.

content.authorization_basis: Original synthetic transcript authored for the AI Video Discovery project. No real video exists.

segments.text: I've been painting the same view for six days now.
It's the corner outside my window, a bakery, a lamppost, a row of brick houses and a crooked plane tree.
And I've been painting it at a different hour each day, with exactly three tubes of paint.
Ultramarine blue, burnt sienna and yellow ochre, plus white.
Today I want to show you all six side by side and explain why limiting myself like
this taught me more about light than any amount of colour I've ever squeezed onto a palette.
First, why three colours. When you only have three, you can't reach for a tube to solve a problem.
If I want a green for the tree, I have to mix it from blue and ochre,
and that green is automatically a bit muted, a bit earthy, which is exactly what a real city tree looks like.
The limitation does the harmonising for me.
Everything in the painting is related, because everything is made from the same three parents.
Second, and this is the real lesson.
Painting the same subject at six times of day forces you to separate two things that beginners, including me, mix up all the time.
The local colour of an object, and the colour of the light hitting it. Look at the bakery wall.
Its local colour is a pale cream.
But at six in the morning, under a grey blue sky, I mixed it with a lot of ultramarine and white.
It's practically lilac. At noon, in direct sun, it's almost pure white with a hint of ochre.
And at seven in the evening, with low orange light, it's a warm pink, mostly burnt sienna and white.
Same wall. Three completely different mixes. If I'd painted what I knew, cream, I'd have got all three wrong.
Third, shadows.
There's a rule of thumb you'll hear, that warm light makes cool shadows and cool light makes warm shadows.
It's broadly true outdoors, because on a sunny day the shadows are lit mostly by the blue sky rather than by the sun.
You can see it in the noon painting.
The shadow under the bakery awning is a cool violet grey, ultramarine with a touch of sienna to knock it down.
But here's where I want to be honest, because the rule is not a law.
In the evening painting, the shadows aren't cool at all.
They're a warm brown, because the light bouncing off those brick houses fills them in.
So I'd rather you learn to look than learn the rule. Fourth, value. Squint at all six.
What you'll notice is that at noon, the range from lightest to darkest is huge, nearly the full range the paint can do.
At dusk, everything is compressed into the middle and dark values, and only the lamppost and the bakery window are light.
That's actually what makes the dusk painting feel like dusk, more than the colour.
If you got the values right and painted it in grey, you'd still know what time it was.
And finally, the one I'm least happy with. The two in the afternoon painting. It's flat.
I think it's because the light was overhead and diffuse that day, so there were almost no shadows to design around,
and I didn't invent any structure to compensate. I've left it in, because I think failures are useful.
If you want to try this, pick a view you can see from a window, give yourself an hour per painting,
and choose three paints that include one warm, one cool and one earth. Then paint the light, not the thing.
I'll put a photo of all six in the description. Thanks for spending the time.
